progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b10: judging a case by a concrete benefit, a concrete harm and who gets each; Bt cotton's benefit, refuges and licence fee; "'Evaluate' needs a verdict". From b11: the evidence ladder; how a suppression gene drive is designed to pass to more than half of offspring and could crash a mosquito population; caged evidence only; its uncertainties (resistance, ecology, borders, reversal); "could, if". From b12: biodiversity's three levels; the baseline ("compared with what?"); Bt cotton's species-level gain against sprayed cotton; yield is not a level. From b08: gene flow, selection and allele frequency. From bio-m5 inheritance: a heterozygous parent passes an allele to about half its offspring. Not assumed: weighing as a method, reversibility as a criterion, conditional verdict wording ("to a large extent", "provided that").
progression.startsWith: Compare two biotechnology cases. The video opens: Two genetic techniques.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining that weighing means asking the same four questions of each case (how big is the benefit and how strong is its evidence; which biodiversity level changes and compared with what; can the change be undone; who gains and who carries the risk) and ending in a verdict with a condition; weighing Bt cotton (large measured benefit; a species-level gain against sprayed cotton; resistance slowed by refuges; no fertile hybrids with native cottons; growers could stop planting it, with more spraying) and the malaria gene drive (enormous need but caged evidence only; aimed at crashing the population of one kind of malaria mosquito, with local species loss and ecosystem effects both uncertain; spreads by itself, so may not be recallable; risk carried across borders); explaining why reversibility weighs heavily (a benefit given up can usually be regained; an extinction cannot, and alleles that spread into wild populations can be very hard to remove); writing conditional verdicts ("to a large extent justified, provided that ..."; "not yet justified for release; staged trials could be, if ...") and explaining why one verdict for all biotechnology is too broad; stating conditions that evidence could check (resistance monitoring for Bt cotton; target decline, other species and consent at each gene drive trial stage); applying this to an unseen reversibility item and an unseen crop evaluation.
progression.nextLesson: how artificial insemination and artificial pollination compare in their processes and outcomes (route entry bio-m6-b15; b14 is cut by the route review).

teaching.task: Bt cotton has been grown for decades; a malaria gene drive has never left a lab cage. Both promise big benefits and both could change biodiversity. So how do you weigh benefits against biodiversity risks, and reach a judgement you can defend?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why a list is not a judgement (it does not weigh, 2); why Bt cotton's benefit is strong evidence (measured over decades, 3); why its gene stays in the crop (no compatible native relatives, 3); why its main risk is manageable (refuges keep resistance alleles rare, recalled from b10, 3); why the gene drive's benefit is uncertain (caged evidence only, 4); why its risk may be permanent (it spreads by itself, recalled from b11, 4); why reversibility changes the weighing (a regained benefit against an unrecoverable loss, 5); why one verdict cannot cover all biotechnology (the same questions give different answers, 6); why a condition must be checkable (monitoring or trial results can move the verdict, 7). Visible case: one board, two columns, the balance tipping only at the verdict. Video advantage: the same four rows filling differently for two cases; the field lane switching back while the species lane cannot. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; the attempt 2 card is the densest frame and is the task.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Bt cotton has been grown in Australia for about thirty years and a malaria gene drive has never left a lab cage, so the question is whether they deserve the same verdict and how to weigh benefits against biodiversity risks; a list of pros and cons fails to tip a balance, so each case goes through the same four questions (how big and how proven is the benefit, which biodiversity level changes and compared with what, can it be undone, who gains and who carries the risk); Bt cotton fills its column with measured benefit, a species-level gain against sprayed cotton and a reversible risk, while the gene drive fills its column with enormous need, caged evidence, a target population that falls if the drive works with local species loss uncertain, and a spread that may not be recallable; reversibility pulls the two apart, giving two conditional verdicts with checkable conditions. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback, the first contrasting a self-limiting release with a self-sustaining suppression gene drive.
teaching.openingDecision: Two genetic techniques. Bt cotton has been grown in Australian cotton fields for about thirty years. A gene drive mosquito, built to fight malaria, has never left a lab cage. Both promise a big benefit, and both could change biodiversity. So should they get the same verdict? How do you weigh the benefits of a biotechnology against its risks to biodiversity, and reach a judgement you can defend?
teaching.understandingCheck: 9a is an explain item: a self-limiting male mosquito release whose inheritance is given (the gene passes to about half the offspring; daughters who inherit it die before adulthood); explain why the gene is expected to disappear once releases stop, and why stopping releases alone may not remove a self-sustaining suppression gene drive (Revision 3, Codex check 92: conditional wording, because some gene drives are designed to be self-limiting). It tests scene 5's reversibility criterion using b11's mechanism and b08's selection. 9c is an evaluate item: a drought-tolerant modified wheat proposed to replace twenty local varieties, with a cross-compatible wild grass at the field edges; evaluate the proposal, weighing benefits against biodiversity effects. It tests the full route stop (four questions, a verdict with its condition) on a new case. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): answer, key reasons, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B6-IQ2-01: "investigate the uses and applications of biotechnology (past, present and future), including: (ACSBL087)", with the listed sub-points this video carries: "evaluating the changes to the Earth's biodiversity due to genetic techniques" (the weighing half; b12 owns the tracing half) and a return to "evaluating the potential benefits for society of research using genetic technologies" (first covered in b11). B6-IQ3-06: "evaluate the effect on biodiversity of using biotechnology in agriculture" (the weighing half, with Bt cotton and attempt 2; b12 owns tracing). The sub-point "analysing the social implications and ethical uses ..." is b10's and is used only through its "who gains, who carries the risk" question. Update the ledger rows when this design passes review. The verbs: "evaluate" is carried by scene 6's verdicts and attempt 2 (what-markers-reward: "Evaluate ... test the thing named in the question against the evidence and reach a supported judgement"); attempt 1 uses "explain" (what-markers-reward: "name the relevant feature, then show how it causes the stated outcome"). The HSC marker-reported faults "generic claims about biotechnology without explaining its actual effect on biodiversity" (2019 Q24) and "a judgement about society without identifying specific technologies and their effects" (2024 Q34, 2025 Q30(b)) (`../research/question-types-bio-m6.md`) are what the four questions and the two named cases target.

design.visualSystem: One weighing board from scene 2 to scene 7: four horizontal rows with small grey labels, top to bottom "benefit: how big, how proven?", "biodiversity: which level, compared with what?", "can it be undone?", "who gains, who carries the risk?", and two case columns headed by painted plates, `m6-bt-cotton-v1.png` (left) and `m5x-anopheles-mosquito-v1.png` (right), each column ending in a small coded balance that tips only when the verdict lands. Cells fill with short grey chips on their cues; the active chip is bright and dims when the next writes. b11's evidence ladder returns as a small thumbnail in the benefit row (Bt cotton on the top rung, the mosquito on "works in animals"), and b12's levels board returns as a small three-row icon in the biodiversity row, so earlier tools are visibly reused rather than redrawn. The reversibility contrast (scene 5) is a coded two-lane strip: a field lane that switches crop and back across season ticks, and a species lane whose silhouette fades and cannot return (a dashed return arrow that stops short). Real objects are painted plates: `m6-bt-cotton-v1.png`, `m6-helicoverpa-larva-boll-v1.png`, `m5x-anopheles-mosquito-v1.png`, the b11 plate `m6-mosquito-cage-v1.png`, `m8-world-map-v1.png`, and for the attempts the new `m6-aedes-mosquito-v1.png` and `m6-wheat-local-varieties-v1.png`, plus `m6-seed-bank-vault-v1.png` in feedback. Gene and inheritance diagrams are b11's clean chromosome panels (`ChromoPair`: two slim homologue outlines, an amber band for the allele), never letter tiles, never painted cells. No people, no body outlines, no hands. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides the small grey row labels; each chip dims when the next cue lands; the column not being discussed dims to grey.
design.transitionPlan: The cotton and mosquito plates open the hook with their grey tags and an untipped balance; the weighing board draws its four row labels one per question while the pros-and-cons list bounces off; the left column brightens and fills its cells with the spray bars, baseline chip, native cotton outline, refuge strip and season switch; the right column fills with the need bar, cage thumbnail, the species row text and ecosystem "?", the drive panel and the border map; the undo strip draws its two lanes and the weights land on a balance; both balances tip as the verdict bars write; the condition weights open into a resistance check bar and three trial check boxes; the memory lines write large; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the card as panels and a small board fill; the decision rule chips and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.

scenes.onScreenChange: four step chips write on in a column, one per cue: "benefit + evidence", "level + baseline", "can it be undone?", "who gains, who carries the risk?", with a bracket to "verdict, provided that ..." and a small grey "checkable?" tag under it on "evidence could check". A "Next" chip slides in at the lower right: "Next: artificial insemination and artificial pollination compared" (small `m6-insemination-straw-tank-v1.png` and `b2b-paintbrush-pollination-v1.png` thumbnails). Hold half a second before the notes.
